#3197. Brighter Than The Sun: How Lionsgate Marketing & PR Turned B.O. Around For ‘Sunrise On The Reaping’

In the wake of Lionsgate‘s last Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes hitting a franchise low at the box office, the Santa Monica, CA based studio got very serious — serious about marketing and reaching the younger audience segemts that the conglomerate built their brand upon with franchises such as Twilight and, of course, Suzanne Collins’ Hunger Games.

Three years ago, it looked like the Hunger Games series petered out with a $44.6M domestic, and $100.8M WW opening and final of $166.3M domestic and $363.9M WW. But this weekend in a death-defying act worthy of Katniss Everdeen herself, Lionsgate completely resuscitated the franchise from its rock bottom. Prequel Hunger Games: Sunrise of the Reaping rose like a phoenix, leaving behoind the previous installment’s box office ashes with a great $120M domestic, $225M global opening. Among prequels at the domestic B.O., Sunrise on the Reaping‘s opening was second only to Rogue One: A Star Wars Story‘s $155M start.

That worldwide B.O. on Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes was worse than any installment in another popular YA franchise; the Harry Potter prequel/spinoff series Fantastic Beasts hit a low wih the last film, 2022’s The Secrets of Dumbledore, at $407.1M. Songbirds & Snakes repped the first time that Collins had written an origins story about one of the core characters, specifically, its villain Coriolanus Snow in a mentorship love story with District 12 tribute Lucy Gray Baird. There was a big bluegrass music element in the film, with Olivia Rodrigo on the soundtrack. Lacking, however, was an OG cast member from the first four films, given that it took place 64 years before the events of the initial Hunger Games novel. Watch on Deadline

The novel was flat out rejected by fans, some pointing to Covid as an easy reason, others to the fact that it was about the bad guy, with 500K first week copies sold and final reported figure of 2.5M. Complicating business further was the fact that Songbirds & Snakes opened at the box office shortly after the actors strike ended. Even though Lionsgate, as an indie studio, had a SAG-AFTRA waiver for the cast to promote, it was still a challenge to prop up a tentpole during such times.

Collins marched on and figured out what her fanbase needed, crafting her next novel, Sunrise on the Reaping about the rise of Katniss and Peeta mentor Haymitch Abernathy (played by Woody Harrelson in the first four films). There was an epilogue in the book, not just with the older Haymitch, but Peeta and Katniss as well. It was the novel that fans wanted and they showed their love by snapping up 4.4 million copies around the globe. It was also a good enough roux for filmmaker Francis Lawrence, director on films 2-5, to work from. In a complete one-up from Songbirds & Snakes, Lionsgate brought back the original 2012 pic’s screenwriter, Oscar-nominated Billy Ray, to adapt Collins’ latest.

RELATED: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Album Boasts 29 Songs; Releases Ahead Of Film

In July 2025, Lionsgate saw a changeover in their marketing and publicity with then EVP Strategy and Chief of Staff Amanda Kozlowski, EVP Worldwide Publicity Nasim Cambron and EVP Global Creative Advertising Jack Teed stepping up. Such exec maneuvers ultimately left Lionsgate all the richer with a female tentpole in last Christmas’ Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfriend thriller The Housemaid ($400.4M, first weekend turnout of 18-34 was 63%) fueled by a dish plate smashing social media meme, and of course, the studio’s first billion-dollar grossing movie last summer, the Michael Jackson biopic, Michael.

Kozlowski was promoted to Worldwide Marketing President in May shortly after Michael‘s $218.8M global opening, in addition to Cambron being elevated to EVP, Worldwide Marketing & Publicity and Teed to EVP, Worldwide Marketing & Creative Advertising. Chris Daniel, SVP, Global Creative Marketing and other members of the Lionsgate Marketing team also get shoutouts here for this weekend’s B.O. success.

“There is a new generation of marketing brains who understand how people are communicating with one another and how marketing messages can make an impact. The leaders of our marketing group, digital, media, publicity and creative teams are going 14 months strong with The Long Walk, Now You See Me, Now You Dont, Housemaid, Michael, and they’re not doing things in traditional ways. They’re creating moments that permeate popular culture and get audiences excited and want to share them with their friends,” said Lionsgate Motion Picture Chairman Adam Fogelson today in celebration of Sunrise on the Reaping.

Previously at a Deadline Regal event over the summer, Fogelson told us that, “All of the things when I was growing up in marketing that were sort of held to be certain and true about how you reach an audience, those things, especially for the generations we’re talking about, have changed.” Case in point: Don’t overshare too much in a trailer; if you do, “you’re going to get flat-out rejected,” he added at the time.

RELATED: 13 Changes Made In ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Film From Suzanne Collins’ Novel“Some of the movies that are succeeding that are coming from this generation, they’re telling [a] story in a very different way,” said Fogelson.

The overarching strategy for Sunrise on the Reaping was to make the sixth installment of the 14-year old franchise feel like the biggest games yet, not only reigniting the passion of longtime fans with a fave character in Haymitch, but also introducing a new generation to Panem.

A longtime motion picture marketing exec going back to Universal, Fogelson’s campaigns were always known for being anchored in character. Sources say Kozlowski has a similar philosophy, but also that the exec knows how to sell story and how to sell to a fanbase. At the center of this Hunger Games promo was Joseph Zada nailing a portrayal of a younger Haymitch.

Kozlowski tells Deadline, “From the beginning, Sunrise on the Reaping had a lot to offer Hunger Games fans — a fan-favorite character whose backstory many had long been asking for, the scale and spectacle of the biggest Games ever and a throughline that connected Haymitch’s tragedy to the rise of the revolution that culminated with Katniss. The marketing team combined those elements with a fan-forward campaign rooted in Gen Z and Gen Alpha online culture, peak Millennial nostalgia, activations that brought the world of Panem into our own and a wealth of unforgettable cast and filmmaker moments. As fans ourselves, it’s been gratifying to see moviegoers responding to the campaign with as much enthusiasm as we have for the world that Suzanne, Francis and Nina (Jacobson) have so lovingly created.”

RELATED: ‘Sunrise On The Reaping’ Epilogue Scene Explained: How Everything Ties Together

The drumroll for Sunrise on the Reaping began a year ago when Lionsgate dropped the first teaser to 109 million global views in 24 hours, which became the studio’s second-most-watched trailer ever after Michael, which they had just debuted a few days prior. At the time, that trailer traffic for Sunrise was +48% ahead of Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, an excellent sign.

From there, Lionsgate created a card stacking (to use a Sunrise word) of high-impact reveals and cultural moments all the way up to release. The studio turned the casting announcements into a pop culture even with 16 individual announcements that generated 541 million views and 35.2 million engagements.

When it came to the late campaign unveiling of the 29-song soundtrack, the studio executed a staggered, artist driven rollout with such performers as Noah Kahan, The Smashing Pumpkins, Ella Langley and Gigi Perez. Altogether this part of the pic’s marketing, which sought to expand beyond the franchise’s core, yielded 40 million+ social views and 186 playlist placements.

RELATED: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Review: Is Time Finally Running Out For The Dystopic Game Show Franchise?

A glittery part of the pic’s push was bringing Panem into the real world with immersive activations, fashion and lifestyle partnerships, and cultural integrations. Lionsgate set up Sunrise Gardens installations across 30 countries and six continents including Peru, Sweden, Brazil, South Africa, Denmark, Belgium, Singapore, Finland, London and more, which was picked up across social media.

The marketing also leaned into the pic’s themes of Capitol Propaganda with a customized Election Day activation, spearheaded by Lionsgate EVP Global Paid Media & Analytics, Dani Otero, across CNN and Fox News generating 79M+ social impressions and repping 31% of the Sunrise social conversation the following day.

Timed to Paris Fashion Week, there was the Elegance Is Authority exhibition at the Musée Rodin attracted 10,000+ registrations in 24 hours.

Also, there were beauty and fashion partnerships with Stila Cosmetics and Depop. Stila’s collaboration reached 1,500+ Ulta stores and generating 50 million+ press and organic social impressions.

In appealing to Gen Z and Gen Alpha, Lionsgate embraced creators, platforms, humor and content creators, inviting them to participate in the franchise rather than simply consume its marketing. Specifically, the studio teamed with a 16-year-old viral editor on the franchise’s first official fan-edit trailer, which pulled in 60.3 million+ views on TikTok. A global fan casting contest inspired 7,500+ submissions and 195.6 million+ views on fan-created videos, with participation extending beyond the core fandom to KATSEYE, Zooey Deschanel and Disney’s Stitch.

Toward the end, Sunrise on the Reaping‘s propaganda built to a crescendo of peak nostalgia by paying homage to the old in the new. Lionsgate made a point to rope in OG cast members Harrelson, Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson with bookings on The Tonight Show and Bravo’s Watch What Happens Live.

The result was a great report card of stats for Sunrise‘s push: 1 billion+ owned-social views, 691M TikTok views, and 74 billion+ views of fan-generated content across relevant Hunger Games TikTok hashtags; 1.5 million new followers across the pic’s official social channels with a massive turnout by the 18-34 at 72% in PostTrak exits. The movie was the No. 2 pic on TikTok’s Trending Chart, behind only Avengers: Doomsday. Conversation volume on X was more than 4x than Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes at the comparable point in its campaign. The digital campaign was overseen by Lionsgate EVP, Head of Worldwide Digital Marketing, Briana McElroy.

The campaign for Sunrise on the Reaping generated renewed enthusiasm among women 17-34 who gave it a 36% first choice versus 24% for Ballad of Songbirds and Snake. Women under 25 showed up at 38% for Sunrise on the Reaping per PostTrak exits.

Overall, the media and social reach for the Sunrise push clocked 2.7 billion+ paid media impressions with heavy play on the NFL, NBA, World Series, and shows such as Saturday Night Live, The Voice, Abbott Elementary, The Traitors and the Real Housewives.

RELATED: All The Times Mckenna Grace Channeled Jennifer Lawrence & ‘Hunger Games’ Past During ‘Sunrise On The Reaping’ Press Tour

In the end, Sunrise on the Reaping pulled in 7.1 million admission this weekend stateside per EntTelligence, +122% from the 3.2M opening weekend admissions of Songbirds & Snakes three years ago.

You could say that the odds were greatly in the favor of Sunrise of the Reaping‘s marketing campaign.

#3196. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3194. Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:

In fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

When I think about luxury vehicles, the first things that instantly come to mind are $60,000+ price tags. Thankfully, entry-level luxury crossovers exist, and they’re some of the smartest buys on the market. For my next comparison, I’m pitting the Mini Countryman and Audi Q3 against each other in a head-to-head matchup to see which compact crossover is worth buying.

Each of them has a distinct take on the "sensibly priced" formula, delivering upscale tech, all-wheel drive, and genuine everyday utility without drifting into absurd price territory. It’s actually been years since I last tested a Mini — the electric Countryman EV — so you can imagine how eager I was to get back into the gas-powered 2027 Mini Countryman S All4.

With an as-tested price of $44,250, it undercuts the $51,790 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro by a wide margin. I will say, however, that you can’t dismiss the Q3 just yet, because after a week’s worth of driving, it too impressed me on plenty of occasions.

2.0-Liter MINI TwinPower Turbo Inline 4-Cylinder Engine

22 mpg city / 29 mpg highway / 25 mpg combined

24 mpg city / 32 mpg highway / 27 mpg combined

Frankly, this one’s tough because these compact crossovers cater to completely different tastes, so personal preference heavily influences the decision.

The 2026 Audi Q3 leans heavily into conventional luxury aesthetics, dressed in Malpelo Blue Metallic with the Black Optic package — which shimmers in the light. Alongside the sharp LED headlights up front and OLED taillights in the back, the package makes it look sleek and unmistakably upscale.

By contrast, the 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 embraces a sportier edge and distinctive British flair. It’s undeniably boxier and more upright, yet it’s loaded with personality — I especially love its Slate Blue Metallic paint job with a contrasting black roof and stripes. Even its LED lighting features customizable light signatures to match its charming looks.

Ultimately, it comes down to whether you prefer understated German luxury or retro-modern charm — making this category an easy tie.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Looking at their spec sheets, it’s quite clear that the 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 holds a slight advantage in terms of fuel economy with an EPA-estimated 27 mpg combined (24 city / 32 highway), compared to the 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro’s 25 mpg combined rating (22 city / 29 highway).

In my real-world testing, however, that gap turned into a surprisingly wide canyon. Over 313.6 miles of mixed driving in the Countryman, I averaged an impressive 31.1 mpg overall — easily exceeding its EPA estimate. Better yet, it hit 30.5 mpg on my best short-distance trip and soared to 36.1 mpg on a longer highway stretch.

In contrast, the Audi Q3 struggled to match its window sticker across 243.5 miles of testing, averaging just 23.2 mpg overall. Even on my best long-distance (26.5 mpg) run, it never came close to its 29 mpg highway rating.

If keeping fuel costs low is a top priority, the Mini is the clear standout here, saving you noticeably more at the pump in the long run.

Most compact crossovers prioritize fuel economy and put driving dynamics in the back seat, but not these two. Better yet, I love how both prove you don’t need a massive engine to have fun behind the wheel.

The 2027 Mini Countryman S All4 is my favorite of the two by a narrow margin, packing a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four engine that puts out 241 horsepower and 295 lb-ft of torque. The Audi similarly has impressive muscle under the hood: a 2.0-liter TFSI four-cylinder that delivers 255 horsepower and 273 lb-ft of torque.

What I will say after being behind the wheel of both is that they’re noticeably zippy off the line, with speedy acceleration that makes it effortless to overtake at cruising speed. While the Q3’s powertrain actually surprised me with a smooth delivery that almost makes it feel more like an EV, it doesn’t beat the Countryman when the road starts to curve. The Mini's lower, wider stance keeps it feeling noticeably more planted through corners, preserving that signature go-kart agility it’s known for.

Despite their smaller footprints, these compact crossovers still offer plenty of room to make lengthy road trips a breeze. However, the 2027 Mini Countryman S All4 holds a slight advantage. That’s because it offers 40.4 inches of front legroom and 37 inches in the rear, which beats the 2026 Audi Q3’s 40 inches up front and 36.1 inches in the back. Additionally, they deliver nearly identical trunk space around 25 cubic feet, easily accommodating my electric scooter.

Inside, they take very different approaches to cabin materials. The Audi leans into traditional luxury with genuine leather seating surfaces, wood inlays, and solid soundproofing that keeps road noise at a minimum. Obviously, the higher price of the Q3 is justified by its more luxurious aesthetics.

Mini takes a totally different approach that gives it a charming style that feels genuinely original. It trades classic leather for Vescin leather-free upholstery and knitted textile surfaces on the dash and doors — which I have to say looked funky and stylish at first glance, but they eventually grew on me.

Sure, the Audi comes up a smidge short on rear legroom, but the Q3 just feels noticeably more plush over long stretches. And when I factor in Audi’s smoother, more intuitive adaptive cruise assist on highways, the Q3 edges ahead as the more relaxing cruiser.

Audi needs to prove it’s worth spending about $7,500 more over its rival. But does it?

While the 2026 Audi Q3 doesn’t skimp on luxury amenities, it simply makes you pay noticeably more for them. Even so, I appreciate its crisp 360-degree camera coverage, head-up display that projects driving details onto the windshield to lessen distractions, and seamless Park Assist Plus for automatic parking. Inside, its panoramic sunroof and vibrant LED ambient lighting create a more upscale look at night — while its large blind-spot warning lights mounted right on the side mirrors are impossible to miss in heavy traffic or in the daytime.

However, you’re still getting better value for the money out of the Mini Countryman S ALL4. For starters, its circular 9.4-inch OLED touchscreen display is a sight to behold and runs a far more intuitive interface. Although it ditches the traditional driver’s cluster entirely, the flip-up head-up display keeps distractions at a minimum. I’m also big on sound, and the punchy Harman Kardon surround sound system easily outclasses the Audi's Sonos setup.

Not only does it offer full 360-degree camera coverage, but it also includes a clever Backup Assistant that takes over the wheel and automatically retraces the path I took to get into the spot. And finally, I really love the adaptive LED headlights with customizable light signatures and cornering lights.

When I weigh this robust feature set against that $7,540 price gap, the Mini delivers far more bang for your buck.

Let me finish by saying that I’d gladly buy either compact crossover in a heartbeat with my own money. That said, the 2026 Audi Q3 S line quattro does come up short once the tallies are counted.

If you prioritize traditional luxury materials, a quieter cabin, and a smoother adaptive cruise control system for long highway commutes, it remains an immensely likable daily driver that costs less than the average luxury vehicle. Honestly, despite losing this head-to-head matchup, I would still gladly buy the Audi Q3 — it’s just that the Mini Countryman gives you more for less.

The 2027 Mini Countryman S ALL4 emerges as the clear winner, and it’s the one I’d ultimately pick. Between its punchy driving dynamics, standout real-world fuel economy, sharper OLED infotainment system, and $7,540 price advantage in this comparison, it simply delivers too much personality and value to ignore.

Apple keeps expanding the iPhone line to include new models. And while it’s great that there are more models for differing preferences and needs, it’s also left me missing the days of having one model that was the clear “best.”

#3191. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

#3190. If You Loved 'Yellowjackets,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Yellowjackets is a vibe. The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying. The dual timelines build tension around the story’s many mysteries, and the complex characters (no one’s completely good or evil on this show) make for a lot of surprising plot swerves that feel grounded despite the supernatural implications all around them. If you’re looking for more of that specific flavor of horror, you should probably watch Alive.

Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.

The survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances. They use the wrecked plane as shelter in the withering cold, they scavenge for anything that could be useful, and they ration out the only food they have: Some chocolates and a case of wine. But an early mistake leaves them without any food at all, and slowly they come to the sickening realization that their best chance at survival is to treat the corpses of their friends and families scattered around the crash site as a food source.

There’s no supernatural aspect, but the story has a similar tone of desperation and despair as Yellowjackets. These are people determined to survive in an impossible situation, and they do things that no one outside of their shared experience could possibly understand. The real-life origins of the story add a sense of horror that more than matches the fictional “It” that haunts the girls of Yellowjackets; putting yourself into that very real experience makes it clear just how terrified everyone was. Rent Alive on Prime Video.

If you’re craving more cannibals, cults, and crazies at the mercy of nature itself, here are a few more movies you should check out.

If you want to watch a movie that is essentially an adaptation of Yellowjackets, check out Eden. Even though it was released years before the show, the stories are so similar (albeit largely gender-flipped) that the producers of Eden actually sued, claiming plagiarism (they lost). In the film, a men’s soccer team (and two women on the same plane) crash-land on a deserted island, and as they fight for survival, things descend into, yes, madness and cannibalism as the survivors suffer dwindling food and water supplies and the rise of two violently opposed factions. It’s not nearly as deeply imagined as Yellowjackets, and it doesn’t have the supernatural hints of the show, but if you want a truly similar story, it’s a good choice. Stream Eden on The Roku Channel, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

You obviously cannot discuss Yellowjackets without discussing Lord of the Flies, William Golding’s 1954 novel about a group of schoolboys who descend into brutality and savagery when they’re stranded on a deserted island. The book has been adapted many times, but the 1963 version directed by Peter Brook is still the best version. Brook managed to elicit remarkably naturalistic performances from his young actors, giving the story a realistic tone that is somehow more terrifying than any amount of horror vibes. Stream Lord of the Flies on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

A slower and more haunting story, Picnic at Hanging Rock explores some of the same themes as Yellowjackets in an entirely different way. On Valentine’s Day in the year 1900, several students and teachers from an all-girls private school in Victoria, Australia, head to Hanging Rock for a picnic. Four students head off to explore and fall inexplicably asleep, and then three vanish, along with one of the teachers. Dreamy and drenched in dread, the story never offers any easy answers, and it explores themes of invading natural areas where you’re not wanted, burgeoning (and confusing) adolescent sexuality, and how our fear of the unknowable warps our perspective and often diminishes our humanity. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

You can never really go wrong with a Hitchcock film, and if you’re looking for another story about a disparate group of people forced to make terrifying decisions in order to survive, watch Lifeboat (based on a story by John Steinbeck). One of the director’s most underrated films, it’s the story of a group of survivors in a lifeboat after a German U-boat sinks their ship during World War II (including one survivor from the German boat). It’s a masterful suspense engine that’s not afraid to have its characters discuss the moral and ethical quandaries facing them as they struggle to survive and maintain their humanity under a constant threat of death. Stream Lifeboat on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

If you love the supernatural aspects of Yellowjackets as the girls come to believe a force they call “It” is out in the woods, check out The Ritual. Four friends embark on a hike in the wilds of northern Sweden to honor their deceased friend. When one of them is injured, they leave the marked trail to take a shortcut through the forest—where they are soon forced to shelter in an abandoned cabin, just like the Yellowjackets—and things begin to slide into the terrifying when they encounter a cult worshipping an ancient deity that grants them immortality in exchange for human sacrifices. It’s as if the show was condensed to an hour-and-a-half and the terror quotient was turned way, way up. Stream The Ritual on Netflix.

#3188. Ina Garten Reveals Why She Will Never Do ‘Dancing With The Stars’

Celebrity Chef Ina Garten revealed this week on her Happy Hour podcast that she once turned down Dancing with the Stars.

Discussing fear, overcoming it and whether she had ever turned something down because it was “too scary,” Garten said, “I think I absolutely have…Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars. I thought nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.”

The chef-turned-podcaster explained, “I thought the closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares. I feel like a lot of people would feel like that. I don’t know. That’s so intimidating.”

Guest Rose Byrne agreed, ‘I would be terrified of that.” Watch on Deadline

Numerous other celebrity chefs have competed on the ABC show, including Rocco DiSpirito, Paula Deen and Giada De Laurentiis, the latter of whom broke her toe while practicing for this season.

Despite her resistance to doing the cha-cha on TV, Garten said that generally she’s “made peace with fear,” given that she often finds herself out over her skis.

“If you push yourself enough, then you have to figure out how to deal with fear. I mean, I feel like um it’s always with me. I never get rid of it. It’s like in the side car next to me while I’m going along.”

The Dancing with the Stars finale will air live coast-to-coast for the first time on Tuesday.

Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale has officially started—but keeping track of the best discounts yet to land and figuring out which deals are worthwhile can be a challenge. As an alternative, you can have Alexa give you a heads-up about deals on products you already know you want to purchase, so you don’t have to spend time sorting through the noise.

Then head to the Alexa mobile app and go to More in the top left (the three horizontal lines) > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping and toggle on Deal Recommendations under the Shopping Recommendations options. This ensures you’ll receive notifications for items that appear in your shopping activity.

If Alexa finds an upcoming deal on something in your Saved for Later, your Wish List, or in your Shopping Cart, you’ll receive a pop-up alert on your Echo Show display or see a yellow light ring on your Echo speaker. You can also ask, “Alexa, what are my notifications?” to hear a list of deals it has compiled thus far. You can also say "Alexa, let me know when [product name] goes on sale."

Alexa can detect deals up to 24 hours in advance, so you can either ask it to remind you again when a deal starts or request that it buy the item when the deal goes live. Simply say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” and it’ll charge the default payment and send the item to the default delivery address on your account.

Rescue moss-stained pavers safely, with gentle methods that actually reach the roots

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Damp, shady weather turns even the best-kept patio into a slippery green mess, and reaching for a pressure washer is not always the smartest fix. High-pressure jets can blast jointing sand straight out from between your pavers, pit soft natural stone, and leave behind micro-scratches where moss and algae grow back even faster.

Fortunately, you do not need heavy machinery to get your patio looking clean and safe underfoot again. A stiff broom, a watering can, and a few simple household staples or outdoor treatments are all it takes to lift stubborn green growth without damaging your stonework.

While a power washer strips surface grime in minutes, it only removes the visible top layer of moss and algae, leaving microscopic spores behind in the pores of the stone. Worse still, blasting delicate limestone, sandstone, or older mortar joints with high-pressure water erodes the surface and loosens the pavers themselves.

Gentle cleaning methods work differently. Instead of relying on brute force, they break down the organic growth at the root so you can brush or rinse it away cleanly, keeping both your stone surface and the sand between your pavers intact.

Before applying any cleaner, move patio furniture out of the way, sweep away loose leaves with a stiff broom (avoid metal rakes, which can scratch pavers), and lightly water any nearby lawn or flowerbeds so plants do not absorb soapy or acidic runoff.

Once prepped, choose the method that best suits your patio material:

If you have delicate natural stone like limestone or sandstone, or simply want the gentlest fix, start with a bucket of warm water and a few generous squeezes of dish soap.

Pour the sudsy mixture over the pavers, let it sit for 15 minutes to loosen the grime, and scrub diagonally across the joints with a stiff outdoor brush so you do not dislodge the sand. Rinse thoroughly with a garden hose.

For heavier green buildup on concrete or brick pavers, wet the patio down first, scatter washing soda crystals (sodium carbonate) across the affected areas, and add a small drizzle of dish soap.

Work the paste into the pavers with a stiff brush, then leave it to sit for 24 to 48 hours before hosing it away. Always wear gloves when handling soda crystals, and keep pets off the patio until it is rinsed clean.

Skip this method on natural stone: because vinegar is acidic, it can etch and discolor limestone, sandstone, or travertine.

Mix equal parts white vinegar and water in a watering can or garden sprayer, saturate the mossy patches, and leave the solution to soak for 20 to 30 minutes before scrubbing with a stiff brush and rinsing well.

If you are tackling a large patio or stubborn black-spot lichen, an oxygen- or enzyme-based outdoor paver cleaner saves hours of scrubbing. Apply the solution with a watering can on a dry day, leave it to break down the spores over a few days, and let the next rainfall wash the dead growth away naturally.

#3181. ‘The Gilded Age’ Star Morgan Spector Breaks Down “Exactly The Wrong Time” For George’s [Spoiler] & “Parallels” Between Anti-Monopoly Legislation And ParaBros Merger In Season 4

SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for The Gilded Age Season 4’s fourth episode.

George Russell’s gunshot wound is coming back to haunt him in a way as Season 4 of The Gilded Age reaches its midpoint.

As has been building since last season when George survived an assassination attempt in his home, a troubling laudanum addiction has come to light for the railroad tycoon, whose behavior early on in the season has grown more and more unpredictable.

“I think it is fairly easy, when you have a long-term injury, and you do have lingering pain, to fall into opiate addiction. I think that is a real thing, but I also think George is someone with a really indomitable will. And I think for someone like him, in our story, to slip into the situation, I think there’s something else going on in his life,” Spector told Deadline. “I think that something else is the destabilization of his relationship with Bertha. I don’t think that’s entirely it. I think, after the shooting last season, he’s really having a gigantic midlife crisis. He’s built this enormous empire, and he’s suddenly realized he doesn’t really know who he is anymore, what his values are, and if and if he wants to keep living his life the way he has been, so I think the laudanum comes along at just exactly the wrong time for him.”

George is under extra pressure this season with President Grover Cleveland (Jim Gaffigan) in town and working on antitrust legislature, which would threaten the railroad monopoly he has worked so hard to construct and protect. Add J.D. Rockefeller (Neal Huff) into the equation wanting to cut back prices he pays Russell Industries to transport his oil, and George feels very cornered in business. Spector had hinted that his character was already having a “crisis of conflict” in Season 3. Watch on Deadline

“Rockefeller was this really interesting character, and so we learned more about him from the research. I’m from Cleveland, and he’s originally from Cleveland. And he basically bankrupted Toledo or some city. He ripped them off, but he was also really pious, and he did do the price fixing,” co-showrunner Sonja Warfield told Deadline. “That’s something he did do. He was ruthless in business, but in church all the time. I love to put characters under pressure. I think it’s where the magic happens, and George and the laudanum —Doctor [Erica] Dunbar had actually suggested that last season.”

The tincture of opium was prescribed by the white doctor who attended to George’s gunshot wound after Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica) saved Mr. Russell’s life in Season 3.

“She did say, ‘You know that you can get addicted to it,’ and so we planted that last season, and what I love is that, Morgan plays it just so deftly and just beautifully — this vulnerable side of George. And in the first season we see George, there’s a character who gets down on his knees and begs him, ‘Spare us,’ and now George is is really at his knees [on this],” Warfield said.

RELATED: RELATED: ‘The Gilded Age’ Producers Address George’s Shocking Decision In Season 3 Finale: “He Feels Bertha Made Him Act Against His Instincts”

Will Morris (Will Pullen) turned out to be the man responsible for the attempt on George’s life, and there is history between the two, because Will is the son of Patrick Morris, the business partner of George’s who took his own life in Season 1 after a deal he made with railroad magnate went bad.

A meeting with Daniel Manning, Secretary of the Treasury during the first two years of Grover Cleveland’s presidency is one of the last instinces of Season 4 in which George exhibits normal behavior despite his substance abuse. It’s explicitly established during that chat that President Cleveland thinks “monopolies threaten our way of government.” George wants to meet with the president, and also Rockefeller, to convince the United States leader that he could gain him political backing in New York for re-election, which George things is iffy for Cleveland. Vieweres can’t help but notice similarities with the merger taking place between Paramount and Warner Bros.

“About the merger thing, Julian and Sonia have a really fantastic record of being a little clairvoyant in terms of the things that they choose to take on in these seasons, and I think partly that’s because there are just so many structural parallels between the era at the end of the 19th century and the era we’re living in now in terms of wealth inequality and concentration of monopoly power,” Spector said. “And what’s fascinating is that those structural similarities create really similar consequences, and that’s because of the way capitalism works. These are systemic dynamics, and they play out in similar ways, no matter what time you’re living in. So yeah, I think either Julian is Nostradamus or maybe there are some structural issues with our political economic system.”

George also confronts Rockefeller at the gentleman’s club they both frequent for business and social life, displaying increasingly erratic behavior and raised voice, as he communicates to the oil baron his plan to get President Cleveland on their side.

#3180. The Best Amazon Prime Benefits You Probably Don't Know About

If you’re going to commit to an Amazon Prime membership, you might as well squeeze as much as you can out of the deal. And there's a good amount of juice to squeeze there. The price you pay for Amazon depends on many factors, but regardless of how much you're paying, it's worth it for most people (we've done the math).

If you're on the fence about signing up, consider that Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is underway, and the company is hosting some amazing tech deals. It's a great time to sell your soul—or take advantage of the 30-day free trial—and there's a lot more to your membership than just deals and free shipping.

The standard Prime membership costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, but there are other tiers that some people might qualify for. For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):

Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

Amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

Sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. This grants access to all the standard benefits, such as free delivery, Prime Video with ads, Prime Reading, third-party benefits like Grubhub, and access to audiobooks, e-books, certain games, and Amazon Music.

Amazon Health: Prime users get One Medical access for an additional $9 per month or $99 per year. Through your devices, you’ll have 24/7 access to on-demand virtual care, plus real-life access to primary care offices in a number of U.S. cities. It accepts most major health insurance plans, too.

Amazon Pharmacy: Access to free two-day delivery and other savings on medications.

Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals with ads, which normally costs $9 per month.

Amazon Music Prime: Access to Amazon's Spotify-esque music streaming service (not to be confused with Amazon's other music streaming subscriptions).

Amazon Luna: A cloud gaming platform that offers new free games every month, free downloadable PC games, content, a monthly Twitch channel subscription, and a free channel subscription on Twitch each month for Prime Members.

Amazon Photos: Unlimited photo storage plus 5 GBs for videos and other files (which extends to members of your Family Vault).

Prime Reading: Free access to a rotating selection of e-books and magazines for Kindle or Fire tablets and Kindle apps.

Amazon's First Reads: You get up to two free e-books every month from a curated list of books handpicked by editors.

This Black Friday is a classic example, where almost every Garmin watch is reduced, with only very new models like the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro excluded from the sales.

I’ve picked out 15 deals on the best Garmin watches available right now, from cheaper Forerunners models all the way up to the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro, which is $849 in the Amazon sale.

I've been hoping to see the Forerunner 165 drop to $129, which it has done in the past, but it has stubbornly refused to go lower than $191 so far. Perhaps it will do on Black Friday itself, but this is still a good deal on the watch I'd buy for a beginner runner.

This is not a big discount, but as one of only a handful of watches Garmin has launched this year I'm surprised to see any deals available at all on the Forerunner 70. If you don't need the smart features on the Forerunner 170 (which has music storage, for one), I think the Forerunner 70 is the best entry-level running watch in the Garmin line-up.

This is the biggest percentage discount I've come across on a Garmin right now, and it makes the Instinct 3 AMOLED very tempting as a reliable adventure watch that offers incredible battery life and a distinctive look.

This is perhaps the best deal going on a Garmin right now. It's on of five Garmin deals I've been looking out for this Black Friday, because even though the Forerunner 265 is an older watch, it's still an excellent multisport tracker with a bright AMOLED display, and it even comes in two sizes.

The Vivoactive 6 is a slick-looking smartwatch with impressive sports tracking credentials, as you'd expect from a Garmin. It has dropped as low as $229 in the past though, so a better deal might be yet to come on the watch this Black Friday.

The Forerunner 965 is the best value alternative to newer top models like the Forerunner 970 and even the Fenix line-up. It packs brilliant sports tracking and navigation features into its slim, attractive case, and you'll be hard pressed to find a better watch from any brand for $449.

The Garmin Venu 4 combines the good looks of a smartwatch with Garmin's excellent sports tracking, and even as a marathoner I prefer it to the more sports-focused Forerunner 570, partly because it has a built-in flashlight.

Even at this reduced price I don't think the Forerunner 570 offers better value than the Venu 4 or Forerunner 965, but it does have some more striking design options than those watches, which might swing it for some. It's still a great sports tracker of course, but lacks maps and a flashlight, which is a shame.

The Venu X1 is a bit of an oddity in the Garmin line-up, with its ultra-thin design and short battery life, but it's actually packed with the same brilliant sports and navigation features as you get on the Forerunner 970. At $300 off, it might be the sleeper hit.

If you want the cheapest good alternative to the Fenix 9 Pro, then right now it's the Epix Pro thanks to this deal. However, the Epix Pro has dropped to just $499 in the past, and I still have hope we'll see that price again this Black Friday.

The best overall sports watch on the market, the Forerunner 970 is still expensive even when reduced by $100, but it's well worth its price. It has a sleek, attractive design and all of Garmin's flagship features aside from LTE connectivity.

While this is a good price for a great adventure watch, the fact that the Fenix 7 Pro has been superseded by three rounds of Fenixes at this point makes me hope there might still be better deals to come on it and the Epix Pro. If not, this is still worth looking at as the cheapest titanium Garmin watch with maps and a MIP display in the sales.

Having just tested the Garmin Enduro 4, I'd say the Enduro 3 is the better value buy for sure, because it has all the same key features as the new watch for $200 less in the sales. Those features include the best battery life of any Garmin, thanks the Enduro 4's MIP display and solar panels.

The Fenix 8 is one of my favorite Garmins of all time, partly because the orange color is absolutely gorgeous. Unless you need the connectivity features on newer Fenix models, I'd say the Fenix 8 is also a better value option in sales right now, because it's not missing much else that you do get on the Fenix 8 Pro and Fenix 9 Pro.

Big savings are available on the Fenix 8 Pro line-up right now, with Black Friday following close on the heels of the launch of the Fenix 9 Pro. The new watch has a few upgrades, including an all-titanium case, but the Fenix 8 Pro is certainly a savvier buy thanks to this $350 saving in my opinion.

#3176. ‘The Gilded Age’ Star Denée Benton Talks Peggy’s “Victory Lap” & “Ambitious Tension” In Her Marriage To Dr. Kirkland

SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for The Gilded Age Season 4’s fourth episode.

As if a new house and husband weren’t enough, Peggy Scott (Denée Benton), now Mrs. Dr. William Kirkland, receives a letter from journalist Ida B. Wells about her newly published book in the fourth episode of Season 4 of The Gilded Age.

The recognition for her novel could be seen as the cherry on top of a wonderful new chapter for the journalist, writer and now wife, whose wedding unfolded in episode 403.

“It’s really fun to see Peggy step into her Renaissance woman era. She’s striving so much for the first few seasons. It’s very ‘Don’t believe me? Just watch’ like everything that she’s getting to do in Season 4,” Benton told Deadline. “Since Season 1, she’s like, ‘I told y’all, you didn’t believe me, but it’s okay.’ And now it’s nice to see her do her victory lap.” Watch on Deadline

Peggy is now part of a union, though, and while her star is on the rise, her husband isn’t currently satisfied at his job. An old colleague of his, Dr. Harris (Dennis Haysbert) pinpoints this with William and suggests he look out for an opening back at Friedman’s Hospital, where Dr. Harris practices in Washington D.C. After discussing it with William, Dr. Harris brings it up with Peggy and both sets of parents of the newlyweds present, where he unintentionally causes some ripples.

“It’s also really nice to play with the ambitious tension that I recognize in Bertha, where there [are] these blinders on, and I was really thankful for how radical it was to see her completely lose sight for a time that she was in a pair and in a family,” Benton added. “It’s fun that the audience won’t always agree with [Peggy]. I think it adds a lot of dynamic texture to her not just having to be this moral gold star for the show, which is very limiting, but to have her lose sight of the fact that William is facing his own challenges, like the limitations of racism, not being able to practice surgery in New York and having a patient die because the white doctor didn’t tend to him. It’s not just as limited as a man having trouble with her ambitions. It’s ‘How do they really balance both of their dreams?’”

A very representative moment of such “ambitious tension’ between husband and wife arrives when one of Peggy’s colleagues, Mr. Simms, mistakenly calls her husband Mr. Scott instead of Dr. Kirkland at a reading and signing for her book. This scene stemmed from a real-life incident co-showrunner Sonja Warfield experienced at a writing event.

“I wasn’t even that much of an established writer, but I have always used my maiden name, even when I was married, and he got referred to as Mr. Warfield. And so I thought, what if that happened in 1885? What’s the impact of that? Especially if the parents are around to witness that, and what does that do to your masculinity then?” Warfield told Deadline. “Because men felt, probably, still to an extent, proprietary over their wives, right? Women really were barely dealing with their career versus family back then, and women worked, and a lot of Black women worked or expected to work and had to work.”

During a carriage ride home after the book signing, Dr. Kirkland tries to address the idea of moving to Washington D.C. with Peggy, who holds firm and wonders why they have to uproot at that exact moment. She doubles back and gives William recognition for his work, but she isn’t quite sold on them moving yet.

“Marriage is really about coming together and becoming one, and Peggy has lived a long time as an individual, and she was an only child, and so she got to do what she wanted,” Warfield said. “So, again, like with Enid and Oscar, marriage will be an eye opener for Peggy and William as well about gender roles, to an extent, because he’s the man, and so he’s supposed to have the last word about their lives, and that was what was expected back then. She would have no say.”

Peggy does holds her own when the discussion of children comes up — as it has now multiple times this season before and after she got married via her husband or his mother when she refers to grandchildren. This is, in addition to the lavender marriage aspect of Enid (Kelly Curran) and Oscar’s (Blake Ritson) union, what sets the women on different paths, since Enid keeps poking at the idea of having a child with Oscar, especially after Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) says she sees a glow about Enid signalling she could be with child in this latest episode.

“It’s cool to watch this power couple trailblaze and navigate what power looked like for them and her. Even seeing a woman at that time decide when or if she wants children, even now there’s still a little taboo for those of us who will admit out loud that we are not sure,” Benton said. “And so for a woman at that time to say, “We’ll see,” is wild, and then it’s really cool to see the ways Mrs. Kirkland is kind of right, where she’s like, ‘Listen, Peggy’s a great woman, but is she going to be a great wife to you?’ And what it means to run a household at that time is basically a full time job. lIt’s cool ike that [Peggy’s] getting to represent so many textures of womanhood and femininity.”

Warfield agreed with Benton’s assessment of the character.

“I think Peggy’s character does surprise us, as Denee said in her reaction to things. I think people think will think a lot of things,” the co-showrunner said. “People might get a little bit upset because Dr. Kirkland is a catch, and I’m sure there are going to be women out there who are saying, ‘Girl, if you don’t want him, then… [I’ll take him!]’”
