#3175. These 14 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this new feature here.

iOS 27.3 also comes with a new setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Currently, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the big screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Apple is also testing a new Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

If you watch videos in Apple Podcasts, you can find them in more sources than the Podcasts app. With the new updates, you'll find these videos on Apple TV 4K, select smart TVs, your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even in CarPlay. (Please don't watch video podcasts while driving.)

'How to Get to Heaven from Belfast' is the sharpest eight-episode binge you haven't watched yet

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Too many murder mysteries telegraph their twists a mile away. This scrappy little series takes a familiar setup and pushes it somewhere much weirder and funnier than you’d expect. Three women in their late 30s reunite for the funeral of a childhood friend, only to start suspecting her death was no accident. That’s how “How to Get to Heaven from Belfast” opens — and it might just be the funniest, most underrated show most people never bothered to watch this year.

It premiered quietly on Netflix back in February, earned glowing reviews, and then more or less vanished, skipped by audiences and passed over for a second season despite being one of the smartest things the streamer put out all year. The show comes from Lisa McGee, the creator of the beloved “Derry Girls,” though you shouldn't walk in expecting more Catholic-schoolgirl hijinks. This is a darker, twistier beast: a genuine murder mystery that happens to be laugh-out-loud funny, trading teenage chaos for middle-aged mayhem. Across eight tightly wound episodes, McGee’s razor-sharp writing and a trio of electric lead performances turn a simple whodunit into a story about grief, friendship, and the secrets we bury—all set to a killer ’90s soundtrack.

If you’re ready for a wickedly funny mystery that’ll have you laughing one minute and gut-punched the next, keep reading.

Saoirse (Roisin Gallagher), Robyn (Sinéad Keenan), and Dara (Caoilfhionn Dunne) were inseparable as teenagers in Belfast, part of a tight-knit group of four. Now in their late 30s, they’ve drifted apart and moved on with their lives — until the sudden death of the fourth member of their group, Greta, brings them back together for her funeral.

What should be a simple reunion quickly spirals into something a lot weirder. The women start to suspect that Greta’s death wasn’t the accident everyone’s calling it. In fact, it may tie directly to a secret from their shared past, one they’ve spent years trying to forget.

Determined to find out what really happened, the trio launches an investigation that takes them well beyond Belfast — even landing them at a resort in Portugal — as the past they’ve been outrunning finally catches up with them.

I’ll keep this simple: The show is funny, the mystery is sharp and the two actually work in tandem. Most of the credit goes to Lisa McGee’s writing. She pulled off the same balancing act on “Derry Girls,” where the comedy never undercut the emotional gut-punches. Doing it again here with older characters and darker stakes makes the show feel far more grounded than most mysteries in its lane.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Roisin Gallagher, Sinéad Keenan, and Caoilfhionn Dunne play women who’ve known each other since childhood, and you buy it immediately. They bicker, cover for each other, and slip back into old habits the way real lifelong friends do. Their chemistry is electric—and given how much time they spent together on set, it’s easy to believe that bond carried over off-camera.

Best of all, it’s a self-contained eight-episode miniseries, meaning the whole story is here and it actually has an ending—no cliffhangers. You can knock it out in a weekend without worrying about Netflix abruptly pulling the plug on a resolution.

It didn’t get nearly the attention it deserved the first time around, which is exactly why it’s worth seeking out now. If you want a smart, funny mystery you can start and finish without a massive commitment, it’s streaming on Netflix — so make sure to catch it (and “Derry Girls” too, if you haven't already).

#3172. Report: Apple job listings detail plans for autonomous AI agents

Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the company’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted new job listings that offer a closer look at its plans to develop autonomous AI agents:

In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the company could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how quickly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally launched its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

#3171. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3169. ChatGPT Health feature now works with Mac app, Dots, more

OpenAI relaunched its ChatGPT Health feature over the summer after piloting earlier in the year. Next, ChatGPT Health is set to expand to more platforms, including the Mac app and more.

With user permission, ChatGPT Health connects to Apple Health and supported medical records to provide useful context to health-related questions. The feature currently works in the United States on iPhone, iPad, and the web.

However, a recent notice from OpenAI points to ChatGPT Health coming to many more platforms.

For instance, ChatGPT Health will soon work with the desktop version of ChatGPT for the first time. This would bring ChatGPT Health to the Mac app.

#3167. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety. Headquartered in Tokyo, Japan, the company provides automotive and robotics organizations with software and services to identify cyber risks early, assess their potential safety impact, and protect systems in operation, helping maintain safe, reliable behavior across real-world deployments.

Sleep experts reveal the unexpected culprits that could be behind your middle insomnia

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Here at Tom's Guide, we know that nighttime wake-ups are a big issue for many people. Which is why, if you've found yourself repeatedly awake at 3 a.m. and unable to fall back to sleep, it's time to take a look around your bedroom.

You might not realize it, but elements of your sleep space could be contributing to your disrupted rest — from technology and light usage, to elements of your bed itself. The simple act of removing them might be the difference between another broken night's rest and staying asleep all night.

With advice from two sleep experts, we're exploring why bedroom environment matters, what to consider changing and why those adjustments are important for sleep.

Temperature, light and sound pollution can all stop you from staying asleep all night."People sleep better when it's dark, when it's quiet, when it's cool, when it's free of disturbances [and] when it's safe, says Dr. Aric Prather, sleep scientist and expert at UCSF and BetterSleep. "And so, trying to optimize that environment on those facets, is certainly a step towards a better night of sleep."

While 3 a.m. wake ups have a variety of causes, there are environmental factors that can contribute to them happening, and keep you awake. Here, we explain what they are, and how removing certain items from your room can help.

Both experts we spoke to advised, where possible, to keep work outside of the bedroom. And since many of us work on computers or laptops at home, removing these from your sleep space can help eliminate distracting light sources and potential stress they're associated with.

The Sleep Foundation points out that having electronics near the bed can contribute to nighttime wakeups through the noise and light they can emit. So, we asked Heather Darwall-Smith, a UKCP psychotherapist specializing in sleep and author of The Science of Sleep, if laptops in the bedroom can be impactful on sleep, through the association with work or light from charging cables.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

If it's your work laptop and it's near your bed and you see the light [this can prompt], 'Oh, that's my work laptop.  Oh, God, did I send that email?'

"It's both," she says. "The mind needs to know the day is done. It's like putting work away. It's creating that boundary between work and home," she explains.

Dr. Prather also points out that waking and seeing a light from a laptop charging cable can carry anxiety. "Because if it's your work laptop and it's near your bed and you see the light [this can prompt], 'Oh, that's my work laptop.  Oh, God, did I send that email?'" he says, adding that it can also lead to ruminating over the next day being a work day.

He adds that "some people's computers have fans that are constantly running and there's heat coming out of them. So that can change the the temperature of the room or the temperature near their body."

As temperatures drop over the winter, keeping your heating on overnight can appear to be a sensible way to combat the seasonal chill — but being mindful of temperature is key to avoiding waking up.

“High temperatures in your bedroom can interfere with your body’s natural cooling process, which is essential for falling and staying asleep,” Dr. Hannah Patel previously explained.

But turning your heating off in the lead-up to bedtime — ideally anytime from around 9 p.m. (though that's not a hard and fast rule if you're an early bird or a night owl!) — you'll allow your bedroom time to cool down.

Similarly, sleeping with an electric blanket is another nighttime practice to be particularly careful with.

Not only is it unsafe to keep an electric blanket on all night (the Electrical Safety Foundation International says they should never be used while sleeping), even modern models with built-in protection to prevent overheating, advise turning off before falling asleep.

Removing your phone from the bedroom is something the Tom's Guide sleep team swears by, in part because expert advice suggests that scrolling your phone late at night can cause a state of mental arousal that may lead to disrupted sleep.

Not to mention, a recent study found that every hour spent on screens before bedtime increases the risk of insomnia by a whopping 59%. As Dr. Prather points out, "phones on their own aren't really problematic, but if people can't keep their hands off them, then they are."

And while the jury is still out on how much blue light from screens is really going to affect your sleep, looking through your phone in the middle of the night can stimulate your brain and prolong awakenings.

However, Darwall-Smith notes that she often finds "people are more stressed by taking the phone out of the bedroom than having it there."

If that's you, consider "turning off your notifications, thinking about how checking the screen or getting into live activity on your phone is going to keep you awake," the sleep psychotherapist advises.

It's the literal foundation of your sleep, but you might not have considered that your mattress could be playing a big part in disrupting it.

Waking up with back pain or stiffness, aching shoulders and hips, overheating during the night, tossing and turning, and even waking up coughing and sneezing can all be signs that your mattress is the culprit behind your nighttime wake ups.

"If you're constantly having back pain or your mattress isn't okay... look into it," says Darwall-Smith, though she points out that back pain might be caused by factors outside of your mattress.

Dr. Prather suggests finding a mattress that is "the right comfort for you, and that probably changes as you age," and recommends "one that supports your posture [and] that doesn't cause pain."

However, as Darwall-Smith notes, "sometimes it's not in [people's] control to change their mattress. So what can you do to make the mattress comfortable? You might want a topper." The best mattress toppers can adjust the comfort and feel of your mattress, and even help with regulating the temperature, all without the cost involved in replacing your existing bed.

Having the wrong pillow for your sleep position, one that has lost it's shape and support, is aggravating allergies or is causing neck pain can all contribute to nighttime wakeups.

Research shows a relationship between an uncomfortable pillow and poor sleep. One study looking at pillow performance found that everyone "who reported poor sleep quality also reported poor pillow comfort."

Sheets, meanwhile, might be something of an afterthought, but synthetic fabrics can trap heat and cause sweaty wake-ups — even though the often low price-point can seem attractive.

Dr. Prather says that along with the right mattress, "the quality of the sheets," and their "breathability" as well as "the quality of the pillow, can all contribute to how comfortable people are, and certainly comfort is something that we want to foster when we're trying to get people to sleep well."

Our best pillows of 2026 can help you determine what's right for you and our guide to the best bed sheets sets of the year has options for different sleep preferences, seasons, and budgets.

While a basic alarm clock can be a better option that relying on your phone, if it's visible from your bed it's potentially making nighttime wakeups worse.

"I prefer people to use actual alarm clocks and to try and find non-alarming alarm clocks," says Darwall-Smith. However, she adds that "I prefer people not to look at their clock."

According to research, clock-watching or 'time monitoring behaviour' (TMB) is common in people who experience insomnia, and something that perpetuates the symptoms of the condition.

Looking at the clock when you wake during the night is "only bad news" says Dr. Prather. "I deal with people with insomnia, but most people are looking at the clock hoping that it's later in the night than it is.  And they're almost always wrong."

Being aware that it's not as late as you hoped then leads to "an immediate anxiety or frustration or discouragement, which pushes against falling back asleep," he explains.

Obviously, we're not suggesting getting rid of the main light in your bedroom altogether, and living each evening in a state of complete darkness.

But if you find yourself awake during the night? "You should not turn on big lights," says Dr. Prather. "If you can keep it low light, that's certainly better."

Speaking of light at night, Darwall-Smith explains that "if you're shining light into your brain at 4 a.m., that's not [good]. Because sleep is reset by the light-dark cycle. As we push towards wakefulness, our eyes register light and it's part of what pushes us up into [being] awake."

However, Dr. Prather cautions against "[sitting] in the dark with your thoughts, usually that isn't a good solution." He recommends activities that are sleep supportive, relaxing and distracting, like reading with a book light, or using a Kindle on low intensity.

Being wide awake in the middle of the night is rarely pleasant, but you don't always have to be concerned by a brief awakening.

"Waking up during the night is normal... it's part of sleep structure. Especially as people get older, it would be very uncommon for people to not wake up during the middle of the night," says Dr. Prather.

Darwall-Smith agrees, adding that, "What we're looking at is the quality of what that waking is. If you get up, wander around, go and have a pee, go back to bed, happy days. You get up and your eyes are peeled to the ceiling and you're freaking out, not so happy days."

And though we've covered ways you can help your sleep by adjusting your bedroom environment, the experts we spoke to emphasized focusing on what works for you, and not adding stress by focusing on creating a 'perfect' environment. "We're not looking for perfection. We're looking for good enough to sleep better," says Dr. Prather.

Darwall-Smith agrees: "Perfectionism is insomnia's best friend. And if we're rushing around trying to perfect our sleeping conditions, Well, do we really need to? Good enough is good enough."

We've talked about what to remove, but there are useful products which can help tackle issues with noise, light and comfort that may be impacting your night's rest. You don't need to strive for absolute perfection, consider these as tools for a calmer, more relaxing night. Even better, these three items are all reduced in the Black Friday mattress deals.

In our Ozlo Sleepbuds 2 review we awarded these tiny buds with 4 starts, with our lead tester noting that she "hoped they would drown out noise so I could stay asleep all night. And they do." Right now, you can get a pair for $40 off in Ozlo's Black Friday & Cyber Monday Sale.

This Sabrina Carpenter approved sleep mask is made with 100% mulberry silk and promises total blackout for a night free from light pollution. It's also adjustable to suit everyone, and the wraparound silk means it's soft on your skin and hair. Plus, it has 30% off in the Amazon Black Friday sale.

If your pillow has been contributing to sleep disruptions, consider the Coop Original Adjustable - it tops our best pillows of 2026 guide. That's largely down to the adjustable fill that lets you create the loft and firmness that suits your individual sleep style. Now 25% off for Black Friday.

#3161. Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement



In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

What You Will Learn:

  • How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes
  • How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected
  • How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures
  • When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material
  • How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects

You can spend plenty of time getting your Mac, display, and desk just right. But what about the chair you use every day? Between typing, taking video calls, and leaning back to watch something, your position changes throughout the day. Your chair should be able to keep up.

That’s the idea behind LiberNovo’s ergonomic chairs, which combine support that moves with you and a choice of sizes, including the Maxis range for bigger and taller users. For Black Friday, LiberNovo is taking up to 42% off in the U.S., with chairs starting at $609 and offers running November 19–30.

Adjusting a chair for your desk is one thing. Keeping that support as you change position is another. LiberNovo’s Dynamic Support System links the neck support, backrest, armrests, and seat so they move together as you recline.

The Bionic FlexFit Backrest adds eight flexible panels that contour independently. Rather than relying on a single rigid backrest, the design lets different sections follow your back as you shift or turn. Once you’ve adjusted the chair to fit, the system is designed to maintain contact through those movements with fewer manual readjustments.

Both the Omni and Maxis families offer five recline positions: 105, 115, 125, 135, and 160 degrees. That gives you options for desk work, a more relaxed position for watching a video, and a deeper recline for a break.

A higher weight limit is only part of finding a chair that fits. Taller users also need enough seat depth, a headrest that reaches the right spot, and armrests with room to adjust.

The LiberNovo Maxis range addresses those details with a 52 cm seat depth, a wider backrest with a flared base, and an extended-travel headrest with 140 mm of vertical adjustment and 120 mm of front-to-back adjustment. Its armrests sit lower and offer a wider, longer adjustment range to accommodate larger builds.

LiberNovo recommends Maxis for users approximately 5 feet 10 inches to 6 feet 7 inches tall, with a maximum supported weight of 399 pounds. Maxis is certified to BIFMA X5.11. The seat cushion uses firmer support at the rear and a softer front edge, while a six-spring Controlled Recline System is designed to build resistance progressively as you lean back.

For a shallower seat, the Omni family offers 45 cm and 48 cm configurations. Choosing between the two families starts with fit, then comes down to which features you want.

There are three feature tiers in each family. Omni SE and Maxis Manual offer manually adjusted lumbar support, without a motor or battery. Both retain the flexible backrest, dynamic support, and five recline positions.

The Maxis Electric includes motorized lumbar adjustment and OmniStretch, a five-minute powered stretch sequence used in deep recline.

Omni Pro and Maxis Airflow add Active AirFlow seat ventilation. A fan draws air through the cushion to carry heat away, and an occupancy sensor pauses the fan when you stand up. These models also include a larger 3,000 mAh rechargeable battery.

Which 18th generation Pro Max phone has the best cameras?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max isn't the only 18 Pro Max to be released this year, now that Xiaomi has just revealed the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max flagships. The two phones share more than just a name, though, and it seems Xiaomi has adopted a very Apple-looking camera bump on the back of its phones. But considering the camera specs are totally different, I started wondering what the actual quality differences were.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is one of the best camera phones, sporting a trio of 48MP camera lenses: one main, with variable aperture, an ultrawide angle, and a telephoto lens with 4x optical zoom. The zooming camera offers up to 16x "optical quality" and has a maximum magnification of 40x. The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, on the other hand, has a 200MP main lens, a 50MP ultrawide and a 200MP telephoto with 3.2x optical zoom.

You'd think that the higher resolution camera would produce the best photos, right? Well we've seen time and again that resolution doesn't always equal quality, especially now that camera phones rely on software just as much as they do hardware. That's why phones like the iPhone 18 Pro Max perform so well in our photo shootouts.

But obviously the only way to find out for sure is to actually take some photos and compare the results from each phone. So, out of iPhone 18 Pro Max and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which 18 Pro Max actually has the best cameras?

The latest and best iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro Max comes with a new variable aperture camera, a larger battery, incredible performance from the A20 Pro chipset and all those other things that make the iPhone worth owning.

The main camera shot is quite different on both phones. The Xiaomi certainly excels in taking a brighter photo, but the result means that the lighter areas look considerably more washed out compared to the iPhone. The overall quality isn't as good either, since the iPhone can pick up more detail in the surroundings, such as my dogs' fur and the gravel on the path. In contrast, the Xiaomi tends to blur those finer details together, especially in the background.

Shooting indoors, things are a little more balanced, but it's clear that the Xiaomi's camera isn't quite as focused as the iPhone's, and most of the Lego set is blurry in comparison to Apple's camera. However the coloring and detail seem to be much closer than they were with the outdoor shot.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

The Xiaomi camera's habit of brightening up the image seems to work in its favor on the ultrawide angle lens, with the iPhone adopting a more washed out and drab-looking color temperature. There are reasons for that, and it all comes down to Apple's automatic white balance being somewhat anti-Fall.

However, coloring aside, the detail on the iPhone-captured shot just isn't there. You can even see it in the grass if you look closely, with all the stalks looking pixelated and blurred, compared to the much sharper detail captured by the Xiaomi.

When it comes to color, the Xiaomi does edge the top spot with slightly more vivid coloring of these berries, in part thanks to the slightly brighter images. The iPhone hasn't washed out the coloring in this instance, and manages to offer a nice bright image with solid contrast between the different colors.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's front camera sports a 50MP sensor, compared to the 18MP one on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, but how much of a difference does it make? As was the case with the rear cameras, the photo is a lot brighter, which really highlights the fact that the sun is shining directly onto my face. Meanwhile the iPhone's shot is a little darker, but the tones seem more true to life and don't make it look like this is my first time outside in several months.

The quality is good on both, even going so far as to pick up the reflection of my other dog in my sunglasses. However, zooming in shows how much of a difference high resolution can make. Xiaomi's rendition of my reflected dog is clear and almost perfect, while the iPhone's is pixelated and grainy. Then again, the rest of the photo is fine, and zooming right in isn't something a lot of folks will be doing.

Xiaomi's Portrait mode is, honestly, incredibly disappointing. The bokeh effect is barely noticeable, and it doesn't really emphasize myself in the same way that the iPhone does. The IPhone 18 Pro Max ramped up that effect to the point where the background isn't that visible, and it makes me pop out a little more. The quality of the photo isn't quite as good, but with the extra bokeh and the return more accurate coloring, it's the clear winner.

Zooming into 4x magnification and things are fairly even. The iPhone's coloring is a little more drab than Xiaomi's, but the overall quality of the zoomed-in shot is basically the same, to the point where it's more about personal preference than anything else.

Jumping up to 8x magnification and you can see how Apple's "optical quality" feature really shines. The shot of my dog at this magnification is much more clear than that of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which noticeably merges the finer details of my dog's fur. The contrasting colors on the Xiaomi's telephoto is more noticeable than the iPhone's, but the loss of quality really lets the team down.

If you increase the magnification to 40x, there's absolutely no question about which camera is better. It's Xiaomi's, simply because the phone produced a clear and crisp shot that the iPhone just can't compete with. I assume some AI upscaling was involved, as is the case with so many other phones, and it's something that Apple consistently fails at. Maybe that's something Apple can include on the iPhone 20.

Going right in with the Macro mode, and the iPhone takes the crown once again. As with before, the picture isn't as bright as Xiaomi's shot, but that doesn't actually matter in this case. The iPhone managed to produce a much crisper photo, with bright colors and details that Xiaomi's camera didn't quite match.

Low light performance can make or break a camera phone, and I'm honestly a little torn over which camera is better in this situation. The iPhone 18 Pro Max produced a shot that is brighter and captured more detail, but it also appears somewhat overexposed in the process.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max managed to capture less detail on the church and its surroundings, despite the higher resolution camera, but produced a shot that looks slightly nicer — so long as you don't zoom in too much. And, honestly, I can't tell you which one I like better.

Overall, the iPhone 18 Pro Max managed to beat out the Xiaomi in more categories, though, the two phones drew in several rounds. That shows that Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's camera is no slouch, but not enough to beat the iPhone's camera in those core categories. The quality of the 8x zoom in particular was especially disappointing, since a 200MP lens should have the resolution to be able to cut down a high-quality image to simulate extra magnification — just like Apple does.

Given the choice, and purely based on camera performance, I'd pick the iPhone 18 Pro Max over the Xiaomi. Still the iPhone 18 Pro Max didn't dominate, and the Xiaomi camera certainly manages to produce some great shots. The fact they tied in four different categories just goes to show that these two phones are both very capable camera phones.

But Xiaomi obviously needs to work on fixing its shortcomings, including capturing more detail in low light, improving the bokeh effect and all those other things that could make the camera even better.

#3158. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

This is a tantalizing, multidisciplinary technology, but the latency issue seems really important. It seems like once they're through the medical hoops national telecoms regulators will have to figure out whether the necessary connections as emergency or critical infrastructure that deserve special spectrum allocation or similar, especially since this seems to have the most promise in more rural or remote settings.

#3157. WhatsApp is raising group chat limit to 1,500 participants

WhatsApp is gradually rolling out an increase to its group chat limit, allowing up to 1,500 participants to join in, instead of the previous 1,024 cap. Here are the details.

While there are exceptions, there are generally two kinds of WhatsApp users: those who hate group chats, and those who can’t seem to be in enough of them.

If you’re in the second category, you’re likely aware that WhatsApp has steadily increased the number of participants allowed in group chats over the years, jumping from 100 to 256 in 2016, then to 512 and, soon after, to 1,024 in 2022.

Now, as spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is once again expanding that limit, raising the maximum number of participants in a group chat to 1,500.

According to the website, the new limit is rolling out to users on iOS and Android, though the rollout is gradual, meaning “not every account will see the higher limit immediately.”

WhatsApp is automatically updating existing groups to support the new limit. This means that admins do not need to take any action to unlock the higher capacity. As soon as the update becomes available to their accounts, their groups will support up to 1500 members. As a result, the update lets admins add up to 476 new members to their existing groups.

This rollout comes as WhatsApp has been working to make group chats easier to manage. Just last month, the company announced four new features, including the ability to pin messages indefinitely, share status updates within groups, filter conversations by mentions and replies, and share recent message history with new members after they join.

To read WABetaInfo’s full report, follow this link.

With top streaming services raising prices seemingly every year — hell, sometimes twice a year — an ad-supported, totally free streaming service like Tubi feels like a Christmas miracle, with over 20,000 shows and movies available to watch without paying a cent. And that sprawling library isn't just about quantity, but quality, too, with content from major film studios including Paramount, MGM and Lionsgate, and television networks including A&E, Lifetime, and Starz.

But to keep that platform feeling fresh and interesting, every once in a while Tubi has to say goodbye to some fan-favorite flicks and series to make room for a new wave of film and TV titles. And with another month rapidly coming to a close (where exactly did November go?), that means you'll have to act quickly if you want to catch these three great movies for $0 before they're gone.

Whether you're in the mood for a weepy autumnal favorite, a beloved Ben Stiller comedy, or a little dystopian trip back to Panem, here are three movies to stream before they leave Tubi soon.

Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, Blythe Danner, and Teri Polo are all back for a fourth "Meet the Parents" movie, "Focker in Law" — with the added fun of Ariana Grande playing a Focker daughter-in-law — which hits theaters nationwide on November 25. If you want to go back to the beginnings of the comedy franchise, though, the original "Meet the Parents" movie is available to watch on Tubi, but not for long.

If you missed the 2000 comedy all those years ago, "Meet the Parents" stars Stiller as the unfortunately-named Greg Focker, who is desperate to impress the parents of his girlfriend (Polo) during her sister's wedding, a goal made significantly more complicated by the fact that her dad is a formidable and overprotective CIA agent (De Niro).

Grab the Kleenex: It's "Stepmom" season. The foliage-filled 1998 weeper stars a Golden Globe-nominated Susan Sarandon as Jackie Harrison, a divorced mother of two who's been diagnosed with terminal cancer. As she battles her illness, she must contend with her ex-husband's new partner, the much younger and career-driven Isabel Kelly (Julia Roberts), who will soon become the stepmother of Jackie's beloved children, Anna (Jena Malone) and Ben (Liam Aiken).

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Though critics at the time dinged the tearjerker for its melodrama ("Solid work from Julia Roberts and Susan Sarandon isn't enough to save 'Stepmom' from a story whose manipulations dilute the effectiveness of a potentially affecting drama," reads the critical consensus on Rotten Tomatoes), "Stepmom" has become an enduring fall favorite thanks to its cozy, family-focused vibes and those iconic leading ladies.

In case you somehow haven't heard, there's a big new "Hunger Games" movie in theaters today: "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," which centers on the 50th Hunger Games, about a quarter-century before Katniss Everdeen's participation.

But before you rush out to your nearest cinema, you can revisit the first installment in the Panem prequels, "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes," which is available to watch for free right now on Tubi. "Ballad" follows an 18-year-old Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth), who tries to restore his disgraced family's status in the post-war Capitol by mentoring Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), a tribute from the impoverished District 12. But will his ruthless ambition get in the way?

Along with Blyth and Zegler, the star-studded cast also includes Peter Dinklage, Hunter Schafer, Josh Andrés Rivera, Jason Schwartzman, and Viola Davis.

#3155. Understand How Satellite Links Shape IoT Device Design and Testing

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.
